paragraphs: The Katha Upanishad tells this story in symbolic language, Swamiji said. Long ago a wealthy man performed a sacrifice that required him to give away everything he owned. But he was not sincere. Hungry for fame, he gave away only what he no longer needed: old, barren, blind and lame cows.

His son Nachiketa saw that his father was breaking his vow. In India parents are honoured almost as gods, so the boy spoke with great respect. Since the sacrifice required giving away everything, he asked, to whom would his father give him? Annoyed, the father brushed him off. Nachiketa asked again, and a third time, until his father snapped that he would give him to Death.

So the boy went to the realm of Yama, the god of death, a pure and holy being who rules over the departed. Yama was away, and Nachiketa waited three days without food. On returning, Yama apologised to his honoured guest and offered him three boons, one for each day. First, Nachiketa asked that his father's anger be gone and that he would welcome him home. Granted. Second, he asked about the sacrifice that leads to heaven. Yama taught it gladly and even named it after the boy.

The third boon was the real question: when a person dies, some say he still exists and some say he does not; which is true? Yama was alarmed. Even the gods had puzzled over this, he said; choose something else. He tempted the boy with sons and grandsons living a hundred years, cattle, elephants, gold, an empire, heavenly music and companions, every desire fulfilled. Nachiketa was unmoved. These things last a day and drain the senses, he replied; wealth cannot satisfy anyone. He wanted only the answer.

Pleased, Yama explained that the good and the pleasant are two different paths; the wise choose the good. He then taught that the Self is never born and never dies, and is not destroyed when the body is. It is not found through clever talk, great intellect or scriptural study alone, but by those whose hearts are pure and senses controlled. Picture the body as a chariot, the Self as its rider, the intellect as charioteer, the mind as reins and the senses as horses: only a well-controlled team reaches the goal. The path is as sharp as a razor's edge, Yama warned, yet one must never despair: "Awake, arise, and stop not till the goal is reached."

Swamiji drew out the lesson for us. Desires multiply faster than we can satisfy them; chasing them never brings lasting happiness. Real life begins when the small, selfish self steps aside and we discover the divine Reality as our own true nature.
learn: Nachiketa shows the courage to ask life's biggest questions and the clarity to say no to shiny distractions. Today's 'boons' are endless scrolling, quick pleasures and status; choosing what is truly good over what is merely pleasant is a skill worth practising daily.
